title: A Word from Our Cleaners
intro: Text 1 is a webpage on which the cleaners of a hawker centre speak to the people who eat there.

visual.text: OUR HAWKER CENTRE · A WORD FROM THE CLEANERS
You carried it to the table. I am 68 — will you carry it back?
Return your tray. It takes you thirty seconds and saves us a great deal more.
An elderly cleaner in a blue apron pushes a trolley stacked high with used trays and bowls. Beside her, a group of students in uniform is getting up to leave a table, their trays still on it.

We are the uncles and aunties in aprons whom you walk past every day. Most of us are older than your parents. When trays are left behind, birds get to the leftovers before we do, the next family has nowhere to sit, and we spend the lunch rush bending, lifting and wiping without a pause. When you return your tray, we can keep the tables clean instead of merely cleared.

visual.title: Three small things
items: Carry your tray, bowls and cups to the nearest return rack
Tip tissues and bones onto the tray, not the table
Halal and non-halal racks are separate — please check the sign

visual.text: “One boy returns his tray and says ‘Thank you, Auntie’ every single day. He does not know that I look out for him.” — Mdm Tan, a cleaner for eleven years
Read more stories from our cleaners

text2.intro: Text 2 is taken from a post on a neighbourhood forum by a secondary school student.
paragraphs: Last Friday my friends and I finished our chicken rice and got up to go, leaving everything on the table as usual. Then I noticed Auntie Rosnah, the cleaner who always hums while she works, stop at the next table and rub her lower back before she bent down again. By the time she reached our corner, a family with a toddler had been standing beside it for five minutes, holding their plates and waiting for a seat.

Nobody had told us to clear up, and nobody stopped us from leaving. That was exactly the problem. I walked back, stacked our trays and carried them to the rack. It took me less time than tying my shoelaces. Auntie Rosnah gave me a small nod, and I felt more embarrassed than proud. Now our group has a rule: whoever finishes eating last carries the trays.

questions.text: Look at the picture in Text 1. How does it support the question asked in the headline?

scheme.answer: It shows an elderly cleaner already pushing a heavy, overloaded trolley while young students walk off and leave their trays, so we see an old person doing the carrying that the students could easily do themselves.
accept: The old cleaner struggles with a full trolley while the students leave their trays behind, which makes readers ask themselves the headline's question: why should she carry what they could carry back?

seeds.text: The picture shows an old cleaner pushing a trolley piled with trays while the students just get up and leave theirs on the table. It shows she has to carry their trays even though she is old, so it backs up the headline asking if we will carry it back.

We see an elderly auntie with a very full trolley and young students walking away from their trays, so the old lady is doing the work the young people should do. This is why the headline asks them to carry their own tray back.
It shows that the hawker centre is very crowded at lunch time.
The picture shows a cleaner at a hawker centre.
An elderly cleaner in a blue apron pushes a trolley stacked high with used trays and bowls.
